stat_summary: In 2024/25, 76% of teachers in state-funded schools in England were female. Only 14% of nursery and primary school teachers were male, compared with 35% of secondary school teachers and 24% of teachers in special schools and pupil referral units, according to the School Workforce Census.
stat_source_title: School workforce in England, Reporting year 2024, Department for Education

male.headline: The Only Bloke in the Staffroom: Just 14 Per Cent of Primary Teachers Are Men, and the Pegs Have Noticed
male.standfirst: New official figures confirm what every male primary teacher already knows from the staff pigeonholes: he is a rare sight, doing a job the country keeps saying it wants more of, and getting precious little for it.
male.image_caption: Tom, 34, putting the chairs up. Still the only bloke on the corridor.
body_paragraphs: New official figures have confirmed what every male primary teacher already knows from the staff pigeonholes: he is a rare sight. Just 14 per cent of nursery and primary teachers in England are men – against 35 per cent in secondary schools – which means a great many children will go through their first years of school without ever being taught by one.
“A parent asked if I was the caretaker, then the PE man, then somebody's dad,” said Tom, 34, from Derby. “I said I was the class teacher. Nobody offered me a lanyard that actually covered it.”

The same census shows the teaching workforce as a whole is 76 per cent female, a figure that has barely shifted in years, even as ministers talk about attracting more men into the classroom. Campaigners are already calling for a National Male Teacher Day, and for a staff toilet that is not, in their words, “down the corridor and through the hall”.
Yet where is the outrage? Where is the recruitment drive that actually works? Britain's scarce primary bloke stacks the tiny chairs, alone, with only a lost cardigan for company.
male.pull_quote: A parent asked if I was the caretaker, then the PE man, then somebody's dad.

female.headline: She Is the School: 76 Per Cent of Teachers Are Women, and They're Still Marking at Half Past Five
female.standfirst: Official workforce figures have finally stated the obvious about who is actually running England's classrooms, and it does not look anything like a short day.
female.image_caption: Sharon, 51, still marking. The tea has gone cold.
body_paragraphs: Official workforce figures have at last stated the obvious about who is actually running England's classrooms. Seventy-six per cent of teachers in state-funded schools are women, and in nursery and primary schools the share is 86 per cent, which means the system is, in any honest reading, being held up by them.

“He came in to do assembly once and went home to a round of applause,” said Sharon, 51, from Plymouth. “I have 30 books to mark, a lost lunchbox and a parents' evening, and nobody's named the staffroom kettle after me.”

Researchers – and anyone who has ever collected a child at the gate – will note that this is not a new pattern, and that women are still slightly less likely than men to be in leadership posts, even while they do the overwhelming share of the classroom work. Campaigners are demanding a Marking Hours Act and a national apology for the phrase “lucky you, finishing at 3.30”.
Until then, the country's unofficial education service will keep stacking the exercise books, one cold mug of tea at a time.
female.pull_quote: I have 30 books to mark, a lost lunchbox and a parents' evening, and nobody's named the staffroom kettle after me.
